title: Data Structures & Algorithms
description: Core data structures, recursion and graph algorithms with complexity analysis.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of reading arr[i] in an array?
questions.e: Elements are contiguous, so the address is computed directly from the index.

questions.q: Which index holds the first element of an array in most languages?
o: It depends on the element type
questions.e: Arrays are zero-indexed in C, Java, Python and JavaScript.

questions.q: Inserting an element at the front of an array of n elements costs:
questions.e: Every existing element has to shift one position.

questions.q: Why is appending to a dynamic array O(1) amortized?
o: Capacity doubles, so costly resizes are rare
The array never needs to resize
Elements are stored in a linked list
questions.e: Doubling makes the total copy cost over n appends O(n).

questions.q: Why is scanning an array usually faster in practice than scanning a linked list of the same length?
o: Better cache locality from contiguous memory
questions.e: Neighbouring elements share cache lines; list nodes are scattered in memory.

questions.q: With two pointers moving inward, finding a pair with a given sum in a sorted array takes:
questions.e: Each step discards one element, so at most n steps are needed.

questions.q: What does each node of a singly linked list store?
o: A value and a pointer to the next node
questions.e: Nodes are chained through next pointers.

questions.q: Accessing the k-th element of a linked list costs:
questions.e: You must walk k nodes from the head.

questions.q: What does a doubly linked list add compared with a singly linked list?
o: A pointer to the previous node
questions.e: The prev pointer allows backwards traversal and O(1) removal given the node.

questions.q: Removing a node when you already hold a reference to its predecessor costs:
questions.e: Only the predecessor's next pointer changes.

questions.q: Floyd's fast/slow pointer technique is used to:
o: Detect a cycle in a linked list
questions.e: If the fast pointer ever meets the slow one, the list has a cycle.

questions.q: Reversing a singly linked list in place needs how much extra memory?
questions.e: Three pointers (prev, current, next) are enough.

questions.q: A stack removes elements in which order?
questions.e: Stacks are LIFO: pop returns the most recent push.

questions.q: A queue removes elements in which order?
questions.e: Queues are FIFO.

questions.q: Which structure does a program use to track active function calls?
questions.e: Each call pushes a frame onto the call stack.

questions.q: Breadth-first search uses which structure to decide the next node?
questions.e: FIFO order visits nodes by distance from the start.

questions.q: How can a queue be built from two stacks with O(1) amortized operations?
o: Push to an inbox stack; pop from an outbox stack, refilling it only when empty
Push to both stacks every time
Sort both stacks after each push
questions.e: Each element moves between stacks at most once.

questions.q: Checking balanced parentheses in a string of length n with a stack takes:
questions.e: Each character is pushed or popped at most once.

questions.q: What must every recursive function have to terminate?
questions.e: The base case is answered without recursing.

questions.q: What happens if recursion never reaches a base case?
questions.e: Frames keep accumulating until the stack runs out.

questions.q: What is factorial(0) by definition?
questions.e: 0! = 1 is the base case of factorial.

questions.q: Naive recursive Fibonacci runs in roughly:
questions.e: It recomputes the same subproblems many times.

questions.q: Memoizing recursive Fibonacci reduces its running time to:
questions.e: Each value is computed once and then reused.

questions.q: Recursive binary search on n elements uses how much stack space?
questions.e: Recursion depth equals the number of halvings.

questions.q: In a BST, keys in a node's left subtree are:
questions.e: That ordering invariant is what makes search efficient.

questions.q: Which traversal visits the keys of a BST in sorted order?
questions.e: Left subtree, node, right subtree.

questions.q: Searching a balanced BST with n keys takes:
questions.e: Each comparison halves the remaining tree.

questions.q: Inserting keys 1, 2, 3, ..., n into an unbalanced BST produces:
o: A tree shaped like a linked list
questions.e: Every key goes to the right, so height is n - 1.

questions.q: AVL and red-black trees keep operations O(log n) by:
o: Rotating nodes to keep the height logarithmic
Sorting the tree after every insert
questions.e: Rotations restore balance after inserts and deletes.

questions.q: Deleting a BST node with two children replaces it with:
questions.e: The successor keeps the ordering invariant intact.

questions.q: An adjacency list stores:
o: A V x V matrix of booleans
questions.e: It uses O(V + E) memory.

questions.q: A graph with no cycles and directed edges is called a:
questions.e: Directed acyclic graph.

questions.q: Which algorithm finds shortest paths in an unweighted graph?
questions.e: BFS explores vertices in order of distance.

questions.q: A topological order exists only for graphs that are:
questions.e: A cycle means no vertex can come first.

questions.q: BFS on a graph stored as adjacency lists runs in:
questions.e: Each vertex and edge is processed once.

questions.q: Dijkstra's algorithm is not correct when the graph has:
questions.e: It assumes a settled distance never decreases.

title: Python Programming
description: From variables to classes: writing clear, correct Python.

questions.q: What is the type of 3.0 in Python?
questions.e: A literal with a decimal point is a float.

questions.q: Which value is falsy in Python?
questions.e: Zero is falsy; non-empty strings and lists are truthy.

questions.q: What does 7 // 2 evaluate to?
questions.e: // is floor division.

questions.q: Strings in Python are:
questions.e: Operations return new strings; the original never changes.

questions.q: What does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluate to?
questions.e: Binary floating point cannot represent these values exactly.

questions.q: After a = [1]; b = a; b.append(2), what is a?
questions.e: a and b name the same list object.

questions.q: Which keyword starts an alternative branch after if?
questions.e: Python uses elif.

questions.q: range(3) produces:
questions.e: The stop value is excluded.

questions.q: What does break do inside a loop?
questions.e: continue skips; break exits.

questions.q: When does a loop's else clause run?
o: When the loop finishes without break
When the loop body never runs, only
questions.e: break skips the else block.

questions.q: What does [x * x for x in range(4) if x % 2 == 0] produce?
questions.e: Only 0 and 2 pass the filter.

questions.q: What does 'a' if 0 else 'b' evaluate to?
questions.e: 0 is falsy, so the else value is chosen.

questions.q: Which keyword defines a function?
questions.e: def name(params): starts a function.

questions.q: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
questions.e: The implicit return value is None.

questions.q: What does *args collect?
o: Extra positional arguments as a tuple
questions.e: **kwargs collects keyword arguments.

questions.q: A variable assigned inside a function without 'global' is:
questions.e: Assignment creates a local name.

questions.q: Why is def f(items=[]) a common bug?
o: The default list is created once and shared between calls
questions.e: Defaults are evaluated once at definition time; use None instead.

questions.q: A closure is a function that:
o: Remembers variables from the scope where it was defined
questions.e: Inner functions capture enclosing variables.

questions.q: Which collection maps keys to values?
questions.e: Dictionaries store key-value pairs.

questions.q: Which collection automatically removes duplicates?
questions.e: Sets hold unique elements.

questions.q: Checking 'x in my_set' takes on average:
questions.e: Sets are hash tables.

questions.q: Which of these can be a dictionary key?
questions.e: Keys must be hashable (immutable).

questions.q: What does d.get('k', 0) return when 'k' is missing?
questions.e: get returns the default instead of raising.

questions.q: Since Python 3.7, iterating over a dict yields keys in:
questions.e: Dicts preserve insertion order.

questions.q: Which method initialises a new object?
questions.e: __init__ runs after the object is created.

questions.q: What does 'self' refer to inside a method?
o: The instance the method was called on
questions.e: It is passed automatically as the first argument.

questions.q: class Dog(Animal): means:
questions.e: The parent class goes in parentheses.

questions.q: What does super().__init__() do in a subclass?
questions.e: It lets the parent set up its part of the object.

questions.q: Which method controls what str(obj) returns?
questions.e: str() uses __str__ (falling back to __repr__).

questions.q: A @property lets you:
o: Access a method like an attribute
questions.e: obj.value calls the getter without parentheses.

questions.q: Which block catches exceptions?
questions.e: Python uses try/except.

questions.q: Which exception does int('abc') raise?
questions.e: The type is right but the value cannot be converted.

questions.q: When does a finally block run?
o: Always, whether or not an exception occurred
Only when there is no exception
Never if there is a return
questions.e: It is for clean-up that must always happen.

questions.q: Which statement raises an exception deliberately?
questions.e: raise ValueError('message').

questions.q: Why is a bare 'except:' discouraged?
o: It also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit and hides bugs
questions.e: Catch the specific exceptions you expect.

questions.q: What does a 'with open(...) as f' block guarantee?
o: The file is closed even if an exception occurs
questions.e: Context managers run their exit logic unconditionally.

title: Databases & SQL
description: Relational modelling, SQL queries and how databases stay consistent and fast.

questions.q: In a relational database, a table row is also called a:
questions.e: Rows are records; columns are attributes.

questions.q: A primary key must be:
questions.e: It identifies each row.

questions.q: A foreign key:
o: References a key in another table
questions.e: It links rows across tables and enforces referential integrity.

questions.q: A many-to-many relationship is usually modelled with:
o: A join table holding two foreign keys
Two primary keys in each table
questions.e: For example enrolments(student_id, course_id).

questions.q: A composite key is:
o: A primary key made of several columns
A key stored in two tables
A key with a default value
questions.e: The combination must be unique.

questions.q: ON DELETE CASCADE on a foreign key means:
o: Deleting the parent row also deletes referencing rows
The parent can never be deleted
questions.e: Dependent rows are removed automatically.

questions.q: Which clause filters rows?
questions.e: WHERE keeps rows that satisfy a condition.

questions.q: Which clause sorts the result?
questions.e: ORDER BY col ASC|DESC.

questions.q: How do you find rows where email is missing?
questions.e: NULL is never equal to anything, even NULL.

questions.q: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM users returns:
questions.e: DISTINCT removes duplicate rows.

questions.q: WHERE name LIKE 'A%' matches names that:
questions.e: % matches any sequence of characters.

questions.q: In which order does SQL logically evaluate these clauses?
questions.e: That is why a SELECT alias cannot be used in WHERE.

questions.q: An INNER JOIN returns:
o: Only rows with a match in both tables
questions.e: Non-matching rows are dropped.

questions.q: A LEFT JOIN keeps:
o: All rows of the left table
All rows of the right table
questions.e: Unmatched right-side columns become NULL.

questions.q: How do you find customers with no orders?
o: LEFT JOIN orders and keep rows where the order id IS NULL
questions.e: The anti-join pattern.

questions.q: A CROSS JOIN of tables with 3 and 4 rows returns:
questions.e: Every combination: the Cartesian product.

questions.q: A self join is used to:
o: Relate rows of a table to other rows of the same table
Join a table to a view
questions.e: For example employees and their managers.

questions.q: Putting a condition on the right table in WHERE instead of ON in a LEFT JOIN:
o: Turns it into an inner join by dropping the NULL rows
questions.e: Filter in ON to keep unmatched left rows.

questions.q: Which function counts rows?
questions.e: COUNT(*) counts every row.

questions.q: GROUP BY is used to:
o: Compute aggregates per group of rows
questions.e: One output row per group.

questions.q: Which clause filters groups after aggregation?
questions.e: WHERE runs before grouping; HAVING after.

questions.q: COUNT(column) differs from COUNT(*) because it:
questions.e: COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULLs.

questions.q: SELECT dept, name, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept fails in strict SQL because:
o: name is neither grouped nor aggregated
questions.e: Each output column must be a group key or an aggregate.

questions.q: AVG(score) over the values 10, NULL and 20 returns:
questions.e: NULLs are skipped by aggregate functions.

questions.q: The main goal of normalization is to:
questions.e: Less duplication means fewer update anomalies.

questions.q: First normal form requires that each column holds:
questions.e: No lists or repeating groups in a cell.

questions.q: A table in 2NF must also have no:
o: Partial dependency on part of a composite key
questions.e: Every non-key column depends on the whole key.

questions.q: Storing a customer's address on every order row risks:
o: Update anomalies when the address changes
questions.e: Some copies may be updated and others missed.

questions.q: 3NF removes which kind of dependency?
questions.e: Non-key columns must depend only on the key.

questions.q: Deliberate denormalization is usually done to:
questions.e: It trades write complexity for fewer joins.

questions.q: What does the A in ACID stand for?
questions.e: All of a transaction happens, or none of it does.

questions.q: Which statement undoes an uncommitted transaction?
questions.e: COMMIT makes changes permanent; ROLLBACK discards them.

questions.q: An index on a column mainly speeds up:
o: Lookups and filtering on that column
questions.e: Writes get slightly slower because the index must be updated.

questions.q: Durability guarantees that committed data:
questions.e: It is written to durable storage before commit returns.

questions.q: A B-tree index supports which queries efficiently?
questions.e: Keys are kept sorted.

questions.q: A 'dirty read' means a transaction reads:
o: Data written by another uncommitted transaction
questions.e: READ COMMITTED and stricter isolation levels prevent it.
